title: RERA Haryana & Real Estate Due Diligence in Gurgaon: Complete HNWI Legal Checklist 2026
author: Adroit Real Estate Services Editorial Team
excerpt: A comprehensive 2026 legal due diligence checklist for high-net-worth and NRI property buyers in Gurgaon. Learn how to verify HRERA registration, title deeds, OC, and BBA terms.
content:
Acquiring premium real estate in Gurgaon and Delhi NCR represents a substantial financial commitment. With ticket sizes for luxury apartments, penthouses, and commercial plots routinely exceeding ₹5 Crore to ₹50 Crore+, thorough legal and regulatory due diligence is not merely a formality—it is the single most important safeguard for protecting capital and ensuring clean asset transfer.

While the implementation of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA) through the Haryana Real Estate Regulatory Authority (HRERA) has brought unprecedented transparency to the Gurgaon property market, navigating complex land titles, developer covenants, municipal sanctions, and registry procedures still demands rigorous professional scrutiny.

In this authoritative 2026 legal playbook, Adroit Real Estate Services outlines the complete, step-by-step due diligence checklist every high-net-worth individual (HNWI), family office, and Non-Resident Indian (NRI) should follow before executing a property transaction in Gurgaon.

1. Verifying HRERA Registration and Project Disclosures

Under Haryana law, any residential or commercial real estate project with a land area exceeding 500 square meters or more than eight apartments must be registered with HRERA Gurgaon.

Key HRERA Verification Points:
• Registration Validity: Visit the official HRERA portal (haryanarera.gov.in) to verify that the project has an active registration number and has not expired or been revoked.
• Sanctioned Plans & Layout Approvals: Compare the marketing brochures and layout plans shared by the sales team against the officially approved building plans uploaded on the HRERA website. Any discrepancy in floor heights, green buffers, or common areas must be red-flagged.
• Quarterly Compliance Reports (QPR): Review the developer's quarterly progress filings. These disclose the percentage of civil construction completed, financial disbursements from the designated RERA escrow account, and pending litigation.
• Project Completion Timeline: Check the committed completion date registered with HRERA, as this determines statutory liability for delayed possession compensation.

2. Title Search and 30-Year Chain of Ownership

A clear and marketable title is non-negotiable. Real estate attorneys should conduct a thorough title search spanning at least 30 years at the local Sub-Registrar's office in Gurgaon.

Critical Title Documents to Inspect:
• Original Allotment Letter & Conveyance Deed: Verify the chain of title from the original government authority (HSVP or DTCP) or primary landowner through each successive purchaser.
• Encumbrance Certificate (EC): Form 15/16 Encumbrance Certificates confirm whether any registered mortgages, court attachments, financial liens, or third-party claims exist on the property.
• Mutation Records (Jamabandi / Intiqal): Ensure the seller's name is properly reflected in the municipal and revenue department mutation records (Revenue Estate / Jamabandi registers).
• Non-Agricultural Land Use Permission (CLU): For township developments, verify that a valid Change of Land Use (CLU) certificate was granted by the Town and Country Planning department.

3. Occupation Certificate (OC) vs. Completion Certificate (CC)

One of the most frequent pitfalls for property buyers is confusing an 'Offer of Possession' with a legal Occupation Certificate.

• Occupation Certificate (OC): Issued by DTCP or HSVP only after inspecting that the building has been constructed in accordance with sanctioned building norms and that essential civic services (water supply, electricity connection, sewerage, firefighting equipment, and lift safety certificates) are operational. Moving into or taking handover of a property without an OC is illegal and leaves buyers vulnerable to regulatory sealing.
• Fire Safety NOC & Lift Safety Certificate: Ensure valid, current clearances from the Haryana Fire Service and Chief Electrical Inspectorate.

4. Scrutinizing the Builder-Buyer Agreement (BBA)

Historically, BBAs were heavily skewed in favor of developers. Under RERA guidelines, developers must use standardized agreements, but critical clauses still demand careful negotiation:

• Carpet Area Definition: Ensure that pricing is anchored strictly to RERA Carpet Area (the net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding the area covered by external walls) rather than ambiguous super area multiples.
• Payment Plan & Milestone Verification: Payments should be linked strictly to physical construction milestones certified by an independent architect, rather than arbitrary calendar dates.
• Penalty Parity for Delays: Under RERA, if a developer delays delivery, the statutory interest rate payable to the buyer must match the interest rate charged to the buyer for delayed installment payments (typically SBI Marginal Cost of Funds Based Lending Rate + 2%).
• Defect Liability Period: Under Section 14(3) of RERA, developers are legally obligated to rectify any structural defects or quality issues without charge for five years from the date of handing over possession.

5. Specific Checklist for Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)

NRIs and OCIs can freely acquire residential and commercial properties in Gurgaon under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA):

• Banking Channels: All funds must be routed through legitimate banking channels using Non-Resident External (NRE) or Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) accounts. Cash transactions are strictly prohibited.
• Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on Resale: When purchasing from an NRI seller, the buyer must deduct TDS at the applicable capital gains rate (often 20% to 30% plus surcharge) under Section 195 of the Income Tax Act, unless the seller procures a Lower TDS Certificate from the tax department.
• Power of Attorney (POA): If an NRI cannot physically travel to Gurgaon for property registration at the Tehsil office, the Special Power of Attorney must be properly executed, attested by the Indian Consulate or Apostilled, and adjudicated at the Gurgaon District Collector's office.
